::: {.solutions}

The TMUA provides **no formula booklet and no calculator**, so every formula here must be *recalled*,
not looked up. Build this sheet up as the course goes (it is started in session 5 and finalised in
session 16), and memorise it in passes in the final week. Nothing here is outside the specification —
if a formula is not on this page, the test will not assume you know it.

A memorisation order that works: **know cold** the ones marked ★ (they appear on almost every paper);
be **fluent** with the rest; and for the two or three you always forget, write them at the very top of
your rough paper the moment the test starts, before you read a single question.

Each section ends with an **exam reflex**: the first move to make when that question type appears. Paper 1
rewards recognition and short routes; if two methods work, use the one with fewer opportunities for error.

---

# Part 0 · The high-yield engines

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 1 · the cards to have automatic</div>
<div class="fs-title">Quadratics, circles and shortest distances</div>
<div class="fs-sub">These three ideas carry more Paper 1 marks than anything else, and they keep reappearing disguised as each other: a tangency question is a discriminant question, and a two-circle question is a distance question. The full section-by-section reference follows below.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Q1 · The discriminant engine ★

For $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ with $a\ne0$, everything is the sign of $\Delta=b^{2}-4ac$:

| $\Delta>0$ | $\Delta=0$ | $\Delta<0$ |
|---|---|---|
| two distinct real roots | one repeated root | no real roots |

$$\alpha+\beta=-\frac{b}{a},\qquad \alpha\beta=\frac{c}{a}$$

**If $a$ can be zero, treat $a=0$ separately** — the equation is then linear with one root.

[$kx^{2}+4x+k=0$ has one root at $k=\pm2$ **and** at $k=0$, for a different reason]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Q2 · "For all $x$" and the sign of $a$ ★

$$ax^{2}+bx+c>0 \text{ for every real } x \iff a>0 \ \textbf{and}\ \Delta<0 .$$

Flip both for "$<0$ for every $x$". **Dropping the condition on $a$ is the standard lost mark.**

Completing the square gives the range directly:

$$a\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^{2}+c-\frac{b^{2}}{4a}$$

— minimum $c-\dfrac{b^{2}}{4a}$ at $x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}$ when $a>0$.

[$x^{2}-6x+k>0$ for all $x$ $\iff$ $36-4k<0$ $\iff$ $k>9$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Q3 · Hidden quadratics ★

Substitute and **carry the restriction with you**:

| equation | let | restriction |
|---|---|---|
| $ax^{4}+bx^{2}+c=0$ | $u=x^{2}$ | $u\ge0$ |
| $a\cdot4^{x}+b\cdot2^{x}+c=0$ | $u=2^{x}$ | $u>0$ |
| $a(\log x)^{2}+b\log x+c=0$ | $u=\log x$ | none, but $x>0$ |
| $a\sin^{2}\theta+b\sin\theta+c=0$ | $u=\sin\theta$ | $-1\le u\le1$ |

*Each value of $u$ that survives gives its own count of $x$ values — two, one or none.*

[$u=x^{2}$: one positive $u$ gives **two** values of $x$; a negative $u$ gives none]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### C1 · Circle — centre and radius ★

$$(x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}=r^{2}$$

From the general form $x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0$:

$$\text{centre }(-g,-f),\qquad r=\sqrt{g^{2}+f^{2}-c}.$$

**It is only a circle when $g^{2}+f^{2}-c>0$** — if it is zero the locus is a single point, and if negative it is empty.

[complete the square in $x$ and in $y$ separately; the leftover constant is $r^{2}$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### C2 · Two circles — the whole classification ★

With centres $C_1,C_2$, radii $r_1,r_2$ and $d=\lvert C_1C_2\rvert$:

| | condition | meeting points |
|---|---|---|
| separate | $d>r_1+r_2$ | $0$ |
| touch outside | $d=r_1+r_2$ | $1$ |
| cross | $\lvert r_1-r_2\rvert<d<r_1+r_2$ | $2$ |
| touch inside | $d=\lvert r_1-r_2\rvert$ | $1$ |
| one inside the other | $d<\lvert r_1-r_2\rvert$ | $0$ |

**Compare $d$ with $r_1+r_2$ and with $\lvert r_1-r_2\rvert$ — never solve the two equations simultaneously.**

[$d=0$ is the concentric case: no meeting points unless $r_1=r_2$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### C3 · Shortest distance between two circles ★

Once the classification is known the distance is a subtraction:

$$\text{separate: } d-r_1-r_2 ,\qquad
\text{one inside the other: } \lvert r_1-r_2\rvert-d .$$

If they cross or touch, the shortest distance is $0$.

*The nearest points lie on the line of centres, which is why only $d$ matters.* The **furthest** distance between the two circles is always $d+r_1+r_2$.

[centres $10$ apart, radii $3$ and $2$: gap $=10-5=5$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### D1 · Point to line — perpendicular distance ★

For the line $Ax+By+C=0$ and the point $(x_0,y_0)$:

$$\boxed{\ \dfrac{\lvert Ax_0+By_0+C\rvert}{\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}}\ }$$

**Put the line in $Ax+By+C=0$ form first** — applying it to $y=mx+k$ as written is the usual error. From $y=mx+k$, use $mx-y+k=0$.

The foot of the perpendicular is

$$(x_0,y_0)+\lambda(A,B),\qquad \lambda=-\frac{Ax_0+By_0+C}{A^{2}+B^{2}} .$$

[distance from the origin to $3x+4y-10=0$ is $\frac{10}{5}=2$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### D2 · Point to circle, and line to circle ★

**Point $P$ to a circle** of centre $C$, radius $r$, with $p=\lvert PC\rvert$:

$$\text{nearest } \lvert p-r\rvert,\qquad \text{furthest } p+r .$$

**Line and circle** — compare the perpendicular distance $h$ from the centre to the line with $r$:

| $h>r$ | $h=r$ | $h<r$ |
|---|---|---|
| misses | **tangent** | cuts twice |

and then the chord has length $2\sqrt{r^{2}-h^{2}}$.

[tangency by distance, or by substituting and setting $\Delta=0$ — the same condition twice]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### D3 · Tangency is a discriminant ★

Substituting $y=mx+k$ into $x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2}$ gives

$$(1+m^{2})x^{2}+2mkx+k^{2}-r^{2}=0,$$

and $\Delta=0$ reduces to

$$k^{2}=r^{2}\left(1+m^{2}\right),$$

which is exactly $\dfrac{\lvert k\rvert}{\sqrt{1+m^{2}}}=r$ — the distance from the centre to the line.

**So "touches" always has two routes.** Use the distance formula when the circle's centre is given, and the discriminant when the question already has you substituting.

[two tangents of gradient $m$ to a circle: the $\pm$ comes from $\lvert k\rvert$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### D4 · Distances you are expected to just know

$$\text{between points: } \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^{2}+(y_2-y_1)^{2}}$$

- **Perpendicular bisector** of $AB$ = the locus of points equidistant from $A$ and $B$; it passes through the midpoint with gradient $-1/m_{AB}$.
- The **shortest distance from a point to a curve** is along the normal — for a circle that is the line of centres, which is why C3 and D2 are subtractions.
- Minimising a distance: minimise $d^{2}$, never $d$. *The square root is increasing, so the same point minimises both, and the algebra is far cleaner.*

[a "closest point on the curve" question with no calculus is almost always a circle in disguise]{.eg}
:::

::::

:::::

::: {.callout-important}
## The three reflexes these cards buy you

1. **"How many solutions / for what values of $k$"** $\to$ form a quadratic and go to $\Delta$. Check whether the coefficient of $x^{2}$ can vanish.
2. **"Touches", "tangent", "exactly one point"** $\to$ either $\Delta=0$ or perpendicular distance $=r$. Pick whichever avoids more algebra.
3. **Any two circles** $\to$ compute $d$, $r_1+r_2$ and $\lvert r_1-r_2\rvert$ **before anything else**. Every question about crossing, touching, containing or gap size is read straight off those three numbers.
:::

## 1 · Algebra and functions (MM1)

**Indices** ★
$$a^m a^n = a^{m+n}, \qquad \frac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}, \qquad (a^m)^n = a^{mn},$$
$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{-n} = \frac{1}{a^n}, \qquad a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}, \qquad a^{m/n} = \left(\sqrt[n]{a}\right)^m .$$

**Surds** ★ — rationalise by multiplying by the conjugate:
$$\frac{1}{a + b\sqrt{c}} \times \frac{a - b\sqrt{c}}{a - b\sqrt{c}} = \frac{a - b\sqrt{c}}{a^2 - b^2 c} .$$

**Quadratics.** For $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$: ★
$$x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}, \qquad \text{discriminant } \Delta = b^2 - 4ac .$$

$$\Delta > 0 \Rightarrow \text{two real roots}, \qquad \Delta = 0 \Rightarrow \text{one (repeated)}, \qquad \Delta < 0 \Rightarrow \text{none}.$$

**Completing the square** ★ — the vertex form gives the turning point for free:
$$a x^2 + bx + c = a\left(x + \tfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2 + \left(c - \tfrac{b^2}{4a}\right), \qquad \text{turning point at } x = -\tfrac{b}{2a}.$$

**Sum and product of roots** (for $ax^2+bx+c=0$, roots $\alpha,\beta$):
$$\alpha + \beta = -\frac{b}{a}, \qquad \alpha\beta = \frac{c}{a}.$$

**Factor / Remainder Theorem.** $\;(x-a)$ is a factor of $f(x) \iff f(a)=0$; the remainder on
dividing $f(x)$ by $(x-a)$ is $f(a)$.

**Modulus (absolute value)** ★ — $\lvert x\rvert = x$ if $x\ge0$, else $-x$; $\;\lvert x\rvert=\sqrt{x^2}$
(never negative); $\;\lvert x-a\rvert =$ distance from $x$ to $a$.
$$\lvert A\rvert = k \iff A = \pm k, \qquad \lvert A\rvert < k \iff -k < A < k, \qquad \lvert A\rvert < \lvert B\rvert \iff A^2 < B^2 .$$
$$\text{Triangle inequality: } \lvert a+b\rvert \le \lvert a\rvert + \lvert b\rvert \quad(\text{equality when } a,b \text{ have the same sign}).$$

- $y=\lvert f(x)\rvert$ reflects the below-axis part **up**; $y=f(\lvert x\rvert)$ mirrors the **right half**
  (even function).
- Two V/Λ moduli enclose a **kite** — area $=\tfrac12 d_1 d_2$ (product of the diagonals, halved).
- $\displaystyle\min_x \sum_i \lvert x-a_i\rvert$ is reached with $x$ **between the two middle points**.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Exam reflex — algebra.**

- A parameter and “two / one / no real roots” $\to$ form a quadratic and use $\Delta>0,=0,<0$.
- “For all real $x$” quadratic inequality $\to$ check the leading sign and the discriminant.
- Symmetric information about roots $\to$ use $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$ before solving the quadratic.
- Several moduli $\to$ mark every breakpoint first, then solve one linear expression on each interval.
- Surd fractions with conjugate denominators $\to$ combine or rationalise before expanding.

**Mini-example.** $x^2-6x+k>0$ for every real $x$ requires the parabola to open upwards and never touch the
axis: $\Delta=36-4k<0$, hence $k>9$.
:::

## 2 · Sequences and series (MM2)

**Arithmetic** (first term $a$, common difference $d$):
$$u_n = a + (n-1)d, \qquad S_n = \frac{n}{2}\big(2a + (n-1)d\big) = \frac{n}{2}(a + \ell).$$

**Sum of the first $n$ integers** ★
$$1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}.$$

**Geometric** (first term $a$, common ratio $r$): ★
$$u_n = a r^{n-1}, \qquad S_n = \frac{a(1 - r^n)}{1 - r} \;(r \ne 1), \qquad S_\infty = \frac{a}{1-r} \;\text{for } |r| < 1.$$

**Binomial expansion** ($n$ a positive integer): ★
$$(1+x)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} x^k, \qquad \binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}, \qquad \binom{n}{1} = n.$$
$$(a+b)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} a^{n-k} b^{k}.$$

::: {.callout-tip}
**Exam reflex — sequences and series.**

- Terms are given at two positions $\to$ write two AP/GP equations and **divide GP equations** to eliminate
  the first term.
- A recurrence looks messy $\to$ generate 4–6 terms and look for a cycle, parity pattern or fixed value.
- A decimal repeats $\to$ write it as a geometric series; do not use a calculator approximation.
- One coefficient is requested $\to$ write only the term(s) whose powers can combine to make it.
- $S_\infty$ appears $\to$ check $|r|<1$ before using it.

**Mini-example.** If $u_3=12$ and $u_6=96$ in a GP, then
$r^3=u_6/u_3=8$, so $r=2$; there is no need to find $a$ first.
:::

---

## 3 · Coordinate geometry (MM3)

**Straight line** ★
$$\text{gradient } m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}, \qquad y - y_1 = m(x - x_1).$$
Parallel: $m_1 = m_2$. &nbsp; Perpendicular: $m_1 m_2 = -1$. ★

**Distance and midpoint**
$$d = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2 + (y_2-y_1)^2}, \qquad M = \left(\tfrac{x_1+x_2}{2}, \tfrac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right).$$

**Circle** ★ — centre $(a,b)$, radius $r$:
$$(x-a)^2 + (y-b)^2 = r^2.$$
General form $x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$ has centre $(-g,-f)$ and radius $\sqrt{g^2+f^2-c}$.

**Circle facts.** The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact; the angle in a
semicircle is a right angle; the perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord.

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
ROOT_CLR, YINT_CLR, ASYM_CLR = '#1f77b4', '#2ca02c', '#d62728'

fig, ax = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(4.2, 12.0))
th = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 400)

def right_angle(a, p, b, size=0.22):
    """draw a small square at the right angle located at p, between directions p->a and p->b"""
    u = np.array(a) - np.array(p); u = u/np.hypot(*u)
    v = np.array(b) - np.array(p); v = v/np.hypot(*v)
    c = np.array(p)
    pts = [c + size*u, c + size*u + size*v, c + size*v]
    return plt.Polygon(pts, closed=False, fill=False, ec='k', lw=1.2)

# 1 — tangent perpendicular to radius
a = ax[0]
a.plot(np.cos(th), np.sin(th), color=ROOT_CLR, lw=2)
a.plot(0, 0, 'o', color=ROOT_CLR, ms=4)
P = (np.cos(0.9), np.sin(0.9))
a.plot([0, P[0]], [0, P[1]], color=ROOT_CLR, lw=1.8)           # radius
tdir = np.array([-P[1], P[0]])                                  # tangent direction
a.plot([P[0]-1.1*tdir[0], P[0]+1.1*tdir[0]],
       [P[1]-1.1*tdir[1], P[1]+1.1*tdir[1]], color=ASYM_CLR, lw=2)
a.plot(*P, 'o', color=ASYM_CLR, ms=5)
a.add_patch(right_angle((0,0), P, (P[0]+tdir[0], P[1]+tdir[1])))
a.text(0.30, 0.34, 'radius', color=ROOT_CLR, fontsize=8.5, rotation=42)
a.set_title('tangent $\\perp$ radius', fontsize=10)

# 2 — angle in a semicircle is a right angle
a = ax[1]
a.plot(np.cos(th), np.sin(th), color=ROOT_CLR, lw=2)
A, B = (-1, 0), (1, 0)
a.plot([A[0], B[0]], [A[1], B[1]], color=ROOT_CLR, lw=1.8)      # diameter
C = (np.cos(1.9), np.sin(1.9))
a.plot([A[0], C[0]], [A[1], C[1]], color=ASYM_CLR, lw=2)
a.plot([B[0], C[0]], [B[1], C[1]], color=ASYM_CLR, lw=2)
for pt in (A, B, C): a.plot(*pt, 'o', color=ASYM_CLR, ms=5)
a.add_patch(right_angle(A, C, B))
a.text(-0.15, -0.22, 'diameter', color=ROOT_CLR, fontsize=8.5)
a.set_title('angle in a semicircle $=90^\\circ$', fontsize=10)

# 3 — perpendicular from centre bisects a chord
a = ax[2]
a.plot(np.cos(th), np.sin(th), color=ROOT_CLR, lw=2)
a.plot(0, 0, 'o', color=ROOT_CLR, ms=4)
yc = 0.45
A, B = (-np.sqrt(1-yc**2), yc), (np.sqrt(1-yc**2), yc)
a.plot([A[0], B[0]], [A[1], B[1]], color=ASYM_CLR, lw=2)        # chord
M = (0, yc)
a.plot([0, M[0]], [0, M[1]], color=ROOT_CLR, lw=1.8)           # perpendicular from centre
for pt in (A, B): a.plot(*pt, 'o', color=ASYM_CLR, ms=5)
a.plot(*M, 'o', color=YINT_CLR, ms=6)
a.add_patch(right_angle((0,0), M, B))
# equal-length ticks on the two halves of the chord
for x0 in (-0.5*np.sqrt(1-yc**2), 0.5*np.sqrt(1-yc**2)):
    a.plot([x0-0.03, x0+0.03], [yc+0.09, yc+0.09], color=YINT_CLR, lw=1.5)
a.text(0.30, 0.12, 'equal', color=YINT_CLR, fontsize=8.5)
a.set_title('$\\perp$ from centre bisects chord', fontsize=10)

for a in ax:
    a.set_aspect('equal'); a.axis('off'); a.set_xlim(-1.25, 1.25); a.set_ylim(-1.25, 1.25)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Perpendicular distance** from $(x_0,y_0)$ to the line $ax+by+c=0$:
$$d = \frac{|a x_0 + b y_0 + c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}.$$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Why — the perpendicular-distance formula

The vector $\mathbf n = (a,\,b)$ is **perpendicular to the line** $ax+by+c=0$ *(the coefficients of $x$
and $y$ are always a normal direction)*. So the distance from $P=(x_0,y_0)$ to the line is the length of
$P$'s displacement from the line, measured **along $\mathbf n$**.

Take any point $Q=(x_1,y_1)$ **on the line**, so that $ax_1+by_1+c=0$. Project the vector $\vec{QP}$ onto
the unit normal $\hat{\mathbf n} = \dfrac{(a,b)}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$:

$$d = \left|\vec{QP}\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\right|
= \frac{\left|a(x_0-x_1) + b(y_0-y_1)\right|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}
= \frac{\left|(ax_0+by_0) - (ax_1+by_1)\right|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}} .$$

But $Q$ is on the line, so $ax_1+by_1 = -c$. Substituting,

$$d = \frac{\left|ax_0 + by_0 + c\right|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}} . \qquad \blacksquare$$

*The choice of $Q$ never appears in the answer — every point on the line gives the same $-c$.*
:::

**Two circles touch** (exactly one common point) when the distance between centres is $r_1 + r_2$
(externally) or $|r_1 - r_2|$ (internally).

::: {.callout-tip}
**Exam reflex — coordinate geometry.**

- Normal to a curve $\to$ differentiate, evaluate the tangent gradient, then take the **negative reciprocal**.
- Perpendicular bisector $\to$ midpoint first, then negative-reciprocal gradient.
- Line meets circle 0, 1 or 2 times $\to$ compare centre-to-line distance $d$ with $r$; use a discriminant
  only if coordinates are explicitly needed.
- Two circles $\to$ compare centre distance $d$ with $r_1+r_2$ and $|r_1-r_2|$.
- Unknown circle parameter $\to$ complete both squares and require $r^2>0$.

**Mini-example.** A line is tangent to a circle exactly when $d=r$; after substitution this is the same as
the resulting quadratic having $\Delta=0$.
:::

## 4 · Trigonometry (MM4)

**Exact values** ★ — know this row cold:

| $\theta$ | $0$ | $30^\circ$ | $45^\circ$ | $60^\circ$ | $90^\circ$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sin$ | $0$ | $\tfrac12$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $1$ |
| $\cos$ | $1$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ | $\tfrac12$ | $0$ |
| $\tan$ | $0$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}$ | $1$ | $\sqrt3$ | — |

**Identities** ★ — these two are the *only* ones the spec assumes:
$$\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1, \qquad \tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}.$$

**Symmetries** (for solving equations over an interval):
$$\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin\theta, \qquad \cos(360^\circ - \theta) = \cos\theta,$$
$$\sin(180^\circ + \theta) = -\sin\theta, \qquad \cos(180^\circ - \theta) = -\cos\theta.$$
Periods: $\sin,\cos$ repeat every $360^\circ$; $\tan$ every $180^\circ$.

**Triangles** ★ — for sides $a,b,c$ opposite angles $A,B,C$:

$$\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C},\qquad
c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C,$$
$$\text{area}=\frac12 ab\sin C,\qquad A+B+C=180^\circ.$$

Use the **cosine rule** for SSS or SAS; the **sine rule** for a known opposite side–angle pair.
With SSA, $\sin B=\sin(180^\circ-B)$ can give **two triangles**; check the angle sum and any “acute/obtuse”
condition.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Range trap.** If an equation is in $\sin 2x$ (or $\cos 2x$) and $x$ runs over $[0^\circ, 360^\circ]$,
then $2x$ runs over $[0^\circ, 720^\circ]$ — **two full turns**, so expect twice as many solutions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
**Exam reflex — trigonometry.**

- Equation in $\sin(mx+c)$ or $\cos(mx+c)$ $\to$ transform the interval first, solve in the new variable,
  then convert back.
- Squared trig function $\to$ split the sign: $\cos^2x=k^2\Rightarrow\cos x=\pm k$.
- Triangle with two sides and included angle $\to$ cosine rule / $\tfrac12ab\sin C$.
- SSA $\to$ test both $B$ and $180^\circ-B$.
- “How many solutions?” $\to$ sketch one period and count intersections, including endpoints.

**Memory picture.** The exact-value table is $\sqrt{0},\sqrt1,\sqrt2,\sqrt3,\sqrt4$ over $2$ for sine;
cosine is the same row backwards.
:::

## 5 · Exponentials and logarithms (MM5)

**Definition** ★
$$y = a^x \iff x = \log_a y \quad (a>0,\ a\ne 1).$$

**Laws of logarithms** ★
$$\log_a(xy) = \log_a x + \log_a y, \qquad \log_a\!\left(\tfrac{x}{y}\right) = \log_a x - \log_a y,$$
$$\log_a(x^k) = k\log_a x, \qquad \log_a a = 1, \qquad \log_a 1 = 0.$$

**Change of base**
$$\log_a x = \frac{\log_b x}{\log_b a}.$$

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Which way up?** $a^x = b \Rightarrow x = \log_a b$, **not** $\log_b a$. Sanity check with size:
$\log_3 2 < 1$ (because $2<3$), while $\log_2 3 > 1$.
:::

**Domains and shapes.** A logarithm requires its **argument $>0$**. For $a>1$, $a^x$ and $\log_a x$ are
increasing; for $0<a<1$, both are decreasing. Their graphs are reflections in $y=x$.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Exam reflex — exponentials and logarithms.**

- Several logs of the same base $\to$ combine to **one log**, then equate arguments; check the domain.
- Different bases $\to$ rewrite as powers of one common base or use change of base.
- $a^{f(x)}=a^{g(x)}$ with valid $a\ne1$ $\to$ equate exponents.
- Nested log/exponential $\to$ work from the inside and write every positivity condition.
- Ordering without a calculator $\to$ compare with landmark powers such as $a^0=1$, $a^1=a$, $a^2$.

**Mini-example.** $\log_2(x-1)+\log_2(x+1)=3$ gives
$\log_2(x^2-1)=3$, hence $x^2=9$; the domain $x>1$ keeps only $x=3$.
:::

---

## 6 · Differentiation (MM6)

**Power rule** ★
$$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\left(x^n\right) = n x^{n-1}, \qquad \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}(k) = 0.$$
Differentiate sums term by term. Often you must **simplify first** (e.g. split a fraction into powers of $x$).

**Uses.**
- Gradient of the curve at a point $=$ value of $\dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}$ there.
- **Tangent** has gradient $\dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}$; **normal** has gradient $-1\big/\dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}$.
- **Stationary points**: solve $\dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx} = 0$. Then $\dfrac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm dx^2} > 0 \Rightarrow$ minimum, $< 0 \Rightarrow$ maximum.
- **Shortest distance** from a curve to a line: the closest point is where the tangent is **parallel to the line**.

**Stationary does not automatically mean turning.** $f'(a)=0$ only gives a horizontal tangent. Classify by
the sign of $f'$ on either side, or use $f''(a)>0$ for a local minimum and $f''(a)<0$ for a local maximum.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Exam reflex — differentiation.**

- Tangent / normal at $x=a$ $\to$ find the point and the gradient separately, then use point–gradient form.
- Max/min of a formula $\to$ differentiate, solve $f'=0$, reject points outside the stated domain, then
  compare stationary points **and endpoints**.
- Optimisation in geometry $\to$ express the target using one variable before differentiating.
- Shortest distance to a line $\to$ tangent parallel to the line; shortest distance to a point $\to$
  minimise the **squared** distance.
- A fraction of powers $\to$ rewrite using indices before differentiating.

**Mini-example.** To minimise distance from $(x,f(x))$ to $(p,q)$, minimise
$D^2=(x-p)^2+(f(x)-q)^2$; the square root is unnecessary.
:::

---

## 7 · Integration (MM7)

**Power rule** ★
$$\int x^n \,\mathrm dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \quad (n \ne -1).$$

**Definite integral** ★
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm dx = \big[F(x)\big]_a^b = F(b) - F(a).$$

**Area vs integral.** ★ A definite integral is a **signed** area — regions below the axis count as
**negative**. To find an actual **area**, split at every axis-crossing and make each piece positive.

**Area between two curves** (upper $-$ lower, over their intersection):
$$A = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \big(y_{\text{top}} - y_{\text{bottom}}\big)\,\mathrm dx.$$

**Translation.** Shifting a graph sideways does not change the area under it:
$\int_{0}^{1} f(x+1)\,\mathrm dx = \int_{1}^{2} f(u)\,\mathrm du.$

**Even & odd symmetry** ★ — an **even** function ($f(-x)=f(x)$) is symmetric about the **$y$-axis**; an
**odd** function ($f(-x)=-f(x)$) is symmetric about the **origin**. So
$$\int_{-a}^{a} f_{\text{even}}(x)\,\mathrm dx = 2\int_{0}^{a} f_{\text{even}}(x)\,\mathrm dx, \qquad \int_{-a}^{a} f_{\text{odd}}(x)\,\mathrm dx = 0.$$
**$f(\lvert x\rvert)$ is *always* even.** Replacing $x$ by $\lvert x\rvert$ makes **any** curve — quadratic,
cubic, or anything else — symmetric about the $y$-axis, because $\lvert -x\rvert = \lvert x\rvert$. Its graph
is the $x\ge0$ half mirrored to the left, so you can **integrate over $x\ge0$ and double** (as in $x^2-2\lvert
x\rvert-8$).

**Floor, ceiling & step functions** ★ — $\lfloor x\rfloor$ rounds **down** ($\lfloor-2.3\rfloor=-3$),
$\lceil x\rceil$ rounds **up**, $\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor\in[0,1)$. Each is **constant on every unit
interval**, so its integral is a **sum of strips**:
$$\int_0^n \lfloor x\rfloor\,\mathrm dx = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}, \qquad \int_0^n \lceil x\rceil\,\mathrm dx = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}, \qquad \int_0^n \{x\}\,\mathrm dx = \frac{n}{2}.$$
When the strip heights scale by a fixed factor, the total is a **geometric series** — e.g.
$\displaystyle\int_0^{99} 2^{\lceil x\rceil}\,\mathrm dx = \sum_{n=1}^{99} 2^n = 2^{100}-2.$

**Modulus integral.** Split at every point where an inside changes sign, and integrate each piece with the
sign it takes there — $\int\lvert f\rvert$ is a true (non-negative) area.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Exam reflex — integration.**

- Simplify first: expand a small product, split a fraction into powers, or use
  $(a+b)^2-(a-b)^2=4ab$.
- Actual area $\to$ find every crossing and split; integral $\to$ keep signs.
- Area between curves $\to$ solve their intersections, then integrate **top minus bottom**.
- $f(-x)$, $f(|x|)$ or symmetric limits $\to$ test odd/even symmetry before calculating.
- Floor/ceiling $\to$ replace the curve by unit-width rectangles and sum the heights.
- A horizontal shift inside $f$ $\to$ change the limits with the same substitution.

**Mini-example.** If $f$ is odd, $\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,dx=0$ immediately—even when the two unsigned areas are
large.
:::

---

## 8 · Graphs and transformations (MM8)

For $y = f(x)$:

| Transformation | Effect |
|---|---|
| $f(x) + a$ | up by $a$ |
| $f(x + a)$ | left by $a$ |
| $a\,f(x)$ | stretch $\times a$ vertically |
| $f(ax)$ | stretch $\times \tfrac1a$ horizontally |
| $-f(x)$ | reflect in the $x$-axis |
| $f(-x)$ | reflect in the $y$-axis |

**Shapes to know on sight:** $y = x^2$ (parabola), $y = x^3$ (cubic), $y = \tfrac1x$ and $y = \tfrac{1}{x^2}$
(reciprocals, with asymptotes), $y = a^x$ (exponential), $y = \sqrt{x}$.

**"For which $k$…" questions** ★ — rearrange to $g(x) = k$, sketch $y = g(x)$, and count how many times
the horizontal line $y = k$ crosses it. The turning-point values of $g$ are the boundaries.

**Sketch checklist** ★ — intercepts; repeated roots; turning points; asymptotes; end behaviour.

- A single root crosses; a double root touches; an odd repeated root crosses with flattening.
- For $\dfrac{ax+b}{cx+d}$, the vertical asymptote is $cx+d=0$ and the horizontal asymptote is
  $y=\dfrac ac$.
- To move a feature through $f(mx+c)$, solve $mx+c=$ its **old $x$-coordinate**. Do not apply the inside
  transformation forwards.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Exam reflex — graphs, transformations and composite expressions.**

- Inside the bracket acts on $x$ and works oppositely; outside acts on $y$ as written.
- $f(x)=g(x)$ $\to$ sketch both and count intersections.
- Tangency $\to$ one intersection $\to$ discriminant $0$ when the intersection equation is quadratic.
- Expression built from an unknown $f(x)$ $\to$ let $w=f(x)$, read the range of $w$, then optimise or solve
  in $w$.
- Max/min on a closed interval $\to$ check turning points **and both endpoints**.

**Mini-example.** If $f$ has a maximum at $(4,7)$, then $f(2x-6)$ has its maximum where
$2x-6=4$, so at $(5,7)$.
:::

## 9 · Paper 1 question recognition

Paper 1 tests the MM1–MM8 mathematics above under time pressure. For the logic and proof language used on
Paper 2, use the **[Paper 2 formula sheet](paper2_formula_sheet.qmd)**.

| If the question says… | Recognise… | First move |
|---|---|---|
| “for all real $x$” | global inequality | discriminant / completed square |
| “exactly one solution” | tangency or repeated root | set $\Delta=0$ or match a turning value |
| “number of solutions” | graph intersections | sketch and count |
| “greatest / least value” | range or optimisation | complete square, let $w=f(x)$, or differentiate |
| “normal to the curve” | two gradients | derivative, then negative reciprocal |
| “area” | unsigned pieces | find crossings and split |
| “integral” | signed area | simplify and use symmetry |
| floor / ceiling | staircase | split into integer intervals |
| two sides and an angle | triangle data | identify SAS or SSA before choosing a rule |
| repeating process | sequence / iteration | calculate a few terms and hunt a cycle |

**Long-question reset.** Write what is fixed, what varies, and the requested output. Then translate the
diagram or wording into one equation. Do not start by expanding everything.

---

::: {.callout-important}
## The exam-day memory dump

Write only what you personally forget. A strong default set is:

1. Quadratic formula and $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$.
2. $S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1-r}$ for $|r|<1$, and $S_n = \dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$.
3. The exact-value trig table (the $30/45/60$ row).
4. $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$.
5. Perpendicular distance $\dfrac{|ax_0+by_0+c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$.
6. Sine rule, cosine rule and area $\tfrac12ab\sin C$.
7. “Inside opposite; outside as written” for graph transformations.
8. $\sqrt{u^2}=|u|$ and every log argument must be $>0$.

**Final check on every answer:** domain · rejected roots · interval endpoints · degrees/radians · exact form.
